We utilize quantum-optical catalysis to generate single-photon facilitated coherent states (FCSs) for continuous-variable systems, leveraging photon correlation induced by an initial catalyst to enhance the non-Gaussian nature of a target mode within a linear optical setting. By employing a 50:50 beam splitter, an initial catalyst shared entanglement is created between the target and catalyst modes; subsequent detection of the catalyst as a single photon yields photon-catalized coherent states (PCCSs) in the target, whose parameters are directly linked to those of the catalyst. We find these resulting PCCSs exhibit non-Gaussian characteristics and phase stability across a broad parameter range, with their degree of coherence matching that of a standard coherent state (GCC). Notably, while the mode function remains Gaussian, the expectation value of the number operator becomes non-Gaussian, and there is a clear dependence on the initial conditions for both the covariance matrix and mean photon number. Furthermore, although no three-mode correlations develop during generation, we observe that spatial mode correlations emerge distinctly from the process. These findings offer a straightforward linear optical method to generate non-Gaussian modes that could advance quantum sensing and communication.

Using the Newman-Penrose formalism, we examine the physical characteristics of the Bivector associated with the Maxwell field, demonstrating that this object is hermitian relative to the null tetrads. We determine its expression through the field strength in a gauge of the Weyl kind and discover a direct correspondence between this Bivector and the self-dual part of the photon's Hermitian matrix. Consequently, every null tetrads arrangement yields an equivalent null rotation around a specific vector that transforms the corresponding Weyl null tetrads. Finally, we establish a correspondence between the Hermitian matrix and a null rotation that transforms any given set of null tetrads into a canonical form, effectively grouping various configurations into distinct equivalence classes governed by the Bivector's intrinsic attributes and alignment with the Weyl metric.

To address this challenge, we developed a novel algorithm utilizing linear regression and integer programming—named the Regression-based Polymer Deduction algorithm or RPD—to predict feasible chemical synthesis from available precursor data. In this study, we applied the RPD specifically to generate a six-unit thiazole-dinedodiazole polymer (RDDZ6). Furthermore, we report the initial report of stable, isolatable dipyrildodiazole bases exceeding five units in length. Finally, we evaluated the RPD's performance against prior experimental synthesis problems, demonstrating its ability to accurately reconstruct known chemical processes.

Although dominant in political discourse on these sites, spatial arrangements have not previously been tested as influencers of misinformation propagation. Our findings substantiate that substantial geographic distributions exist within U.S. Reddit populations and demonstrate that such configurations facilitate wider misinformation reach by disrupting the web's small-world architecture. Specifically, major geographic clusters drastically increase the shortest path web distances for content dissemination—even though posting frequency and site promotion tools were unconsidered in this analysis—which highlights their unique impact. These insights reveal how big spatial arrangements exacerbate the public's susceptibility to false claims.

Additionally, confirming prior discoveries, experiment results show learners acquire manipulation skills more efficiently when instruction includes these non-isomorphic auditory demonstrations.

Users predominantly depend on Google to access information about people, jobs, and businesses, though concerns regarding how results are tailored to individual queries have persisted. This study empirically demonstrates the impact of this personalization: without it, overlooked information decreases significantly. We measured its effects using two metrics—information recall and surprise—across six domains: a healthcare provider, an employer potential, a public official, a convicted felon, a missing person, and a missing item. Data collection involved a randomized sample of 2,000 adults; each participant customized Google for one of these scenarios by querying it three times after seeing an image and some background context. Findings revealed that 37.6% of participants failed to detect pertinent, undeniably important information when search results were personalized compared to 59.2% in the non-personalized condition. These disparities were even more pronounced among search experts, media professionals, and experienced employees. Results hold major implications legally, ethically, and regarding public choice matters by showing evidence that personalization obscures critical data that users encounter in searches when results are tailored to their specific requests.

Recovering friction from internal forces is a crucial step toward understanding how granular beds fail. To investigate this dependency, we conducted force balance calculations using simulated monodisperse cylinders within both dry and wet soft-sphere systems under varying boundary conditions and driving mechanisms that produce different levels of asymmetric drag forces. Our results show that while asymmetry always increases with the intensity of the driving force, specific mechanisms—such as shear-induced particle migration and the formation of dilated channels—suppress it. Consequently, we suggest it is difficult for the 0.44 figure to represent a universal friction limit across systems with distinct internal forces, as the effects of long-range forces like electrostatics or those missing in molecular dynamics simulations significantly alter the observed drag symmetry.

We introduce ContainerLoop, a debugging tool for containerized cloud-native architectures that leverages data flow analysis to automatically synthesize rules, known as time loops, to identify violations of strict ordering constraints between service pairs. Like application-level logic loops, time loops occur when packets circumvent expected routes due to network states, such as standing on a loop in the path, or by being placed into a rule on a different service. Because most protocols operate under a non-blocking assumption, these unexpected sequences can easily give rise to complex bugs that are hard to diagnose. Networks loops, however, follow a simpler pattern: they always involve a non-monotonic state change (one that goes backwards) across at least a three-service path. Our formula easy models this loop and can detect its presence directly from logs produced any system. To validate our approach, we analyzed logs generated by a bug-inducing version, finding that our method successfully recovered the time-loop and simplified the existing debug. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has established itself as a primary driver for advancing large language models (LLMs) across multiple domains. Nevertheless, a vital capability remains largely neglected: transferring insights gained from one task to another. Although this knowledge migration is essential in practical implementations, current approaches often fail to capture critical nuances, resulting in performance declines. To establish a more robust framework, we introduce a flexible, representation-based approach grounded in RLHF that preserves transferred performance more effectively. Further broadening this investigation, we address real-world intricateities by incorporating an unsupervised setting where each task is defined by a pair of boundaries—specifically, unsupervised data that cannot rely on external labels. Within this context, we demonstrate that conventional methods using RLHF face important constraints. In response, we present Retrieval-enhanced Transfer (RetroT), our proposed solution that utilizes retrieval-based updates to feed transferred tasks with unsupervised data preserved through boundary constraints. We validate our findings across three distinct use cases: code generation, mathematical solving, and natural language inference tasks. Experiments involving synthetic and real-world data streams demonstrate how Retrieval-based Transfer outperforms existing methodologies.

Implementing neural network language models with sufficient capacity to capture large-scale language patterns is critical for generating high-quality text. However, this capability often results in excessive parameter counts, leading to significant memory requirements, storage costs, and inference latency. This study introduces Sparse Generative Opponent Network (SparseGAN), an innovative architecture that reduces parameter count while preserving performance. Like a traditional GAN, it employs a role-based approach where a "generator" produces text and a "discriminator" evaluates its authenticity against real data. Experiments conducted using the massive 4.8 billion token Wikipedia dataset demonstrate that SparseGAN matches the blast radius (ability to generalize) of standard Generative Adversarial Networks without a shared dictionary, delivers faster training times, uses less memory, offers quicker inference, and requires significantly fewer parameters.

Emotion-tagging classifies the sentiment hidden within a specific type of inquiry known as an emotion-question. In contrast, tags applied to ordinary, non-emotion-question inquiries classify the corresponding answers. The primary distinction between these two formats is that while regular inquiries are answered with factual information (such as an entity, event, or attribute), emotion-inquiries seek a justification behind the action itself—for instance, asking if a train arrived ("Did the train arrive?") versus whether it was delayed ("Was the train delayed?"). Structurally and semantically, these inquiries diverge significantly, leading current methodologies to handle them separately using disjoint frameworks. Our strategy, however, unifies their processing by leveraging a BERT-based representation for standard questions while introducing new embeddings for emotion-question pairs; specifically, non-emotion entities are represented as token sequences, whereas emotion-emotiers use directed graphs constructed from BERT-derived semantic vectors. However, when dealing with ill-posed problems, extracting unique solutions from views generated by unknown prior mechanisms becomes impossible without assumptions. Without knowing the specific distribution from which data was drawn, designing a suitable model to represent these hidden assumptions during both forward and backward processes is a significant hurdle. Recent advancements in generating speech through automatic neural networks, like WaveNet acting on full waveforms, offer superior quality but often lack complete probability calculations due to their intricate multi-dilated convolutions. This study introduces a novel approach termed Quasi-Periodic WaveNet to address these limitations while preserving high-fidelity quality. The design implements a reversed-autoregressive process where untrained wave-attention networks handle groups of sample audio segments. During training, it functions as standard WaveNet; however, in generation, pre-filled sample lengths are extended one at a time using newly learned contextual probabilities to gradually build the audio. Once an initial audio segment reaches full quality, the training distribution—shifting from data to quasi-stable probabilities—allows for efficient generation in a non-periodic manner. Compared to utilizing multi-dilated convolutions throughout all possible lengths, this model employs dilated convolutions only within shorter length ranges to drastically cut computational costs. Additionally, the system integrates a novel Pitch-Sensitive Convolution Neural Network (PCNN) that adapts generating patterns based on pitch information to generate more natural and authentic speech. Experimental results confirm significant improvements over existing methods, particularly when compared to the Pitch-sensitive CNA Neural Network.

We derive canonical equilibrium conditions by incorporating the integral and differential operators used in the phase space formulation of quantum mechanics specifically for Weyl symbols. The resulting Hamiltonian density functions in the Hughenbaum-Wigner representation are established as foundational for canonical local thermal equilibrium (C-LTE) states, which emerge generally from the C-Boltzman representation in the Weyl symbol space. For both C-LTE states and local thermal equilibrium states, we demonstrate that their associated Weyl-Wigner representations must adhere strictly to specific canonical thermal equilibrium conditions.

In this approach to understanding, we suggest that such systems do not possess these counterintuitive values because they are governed strictly by standard Clausius definitions, rather than alternative formulations which might suggest entirely different physical realities. Specifically, we argue the practice of assigning negative temperatures, while intriguing, reflects an incomplete grasp of standard thermodynamic principles, as it results when one applies the original forms of Kirchhoff and Loschmidts laws in ways that distort their intent.

Furthermore, there is significant emphasis placed upon a strict adherence to time reversal, not just for physical consistency, but to preserve statistical and mechanistic accuracy in these models. Ultimately, if our interpretation holds, these so - called negative values may very well not represent true negative temperatures in the most precise scientific terms, suggesting instead that systems exist at an extremely high, intense positive temperature level that mimics such bizarre behavioral characteristics without actually requiring this specific theoretical label.

We begin by explicitly constructing this model and defining its dark matter thermal relic abundance constraints within a generalized framework. Subsequently, we explore the phenomenology associated with dark matter direct detection as well as collider searches, and analyze the stability of the potential. The results demonstrate rich dark matter phenomenology and indicate that effects from new physics can influence both thermal and non-thermal processes, collisions, detectors on Earth, and observatories situated far away in space.

ViDaExpert serves as a tool enabling nonlinear visual analysis of vector data derived from various sources, including traditional relational databases, neural network outputs, and other formats. It introduces the Refinement Flowchart—a novel nonlinear representation designed to facilitate the comprehensive examination and hierarchical filtering of multidimensional vector datasets. This structure integrates several components: a Refinement Flowchart illustrating global data relationships, Subgraph Charts offering detailed views of intricate chart-type data relations alongside Refinement Paths (guiding sequential focus shifts), and Refinement Nodes (enabling rapid search and filtering capabilities). ViDaExpert proves invaluable for: (1) enhancing the interpretability of multidimensional vector relationships in previously searchable database contents; (2) rendering search results from large-scale artificial intelligence models more understandable; (2) improving general understandability of other forms of directional data. Evidence from laboratory experiments involving AI professionals and guests confirms that compared to mainstream techniques, ViDaExpert surpasss users in usability for analyzing comprehensive dimensions of all-ench user inputs search directions.
